Movies vs. TV Shows on Netflix During COVID-19

MGTS103 Data Visualization Project · Netflix Daily Top 10, April 1, 2020 to March 11, 2022

1. Introduction2. Dataset & methodology3. Visualizations4. Analysis5. Conclusion6. Datasets7. Requirements & checks

1. Introduction

Research question: Did people watch more movies or TV shows during COVID-19?

This project compares how popular movies and TV shows were on Netflix, using the Netflix Daily Top 10 rankings. It looks at how often each category appeared in the Top 10, how highly it ranked, how popularity changed month by month, and how long titles stayed on the chart.

63.0%of Top 10 appearances were TV shows (4,446)
37.0%were movies (2,611)
23 of 24months TV shows had more appearances
9 vs 6median days in the Top 10 per title, TV vs. movies
Important limitation: The data measures Netflix Top 10 popularity only. It is not total viewing time, and it does not cover other platforms. The question is therefore answered as “which type of content was more popular on Netflix?”

2. Dataset and methodology

Source: netflix daily top 10.csv (provided for this project): 7,100 daily records, 10 ranks on each of 710 days. Fields used: date (As of), Rank, Title, Type, Days In Top 10 and Viewership Score.

Cleaning steps

  1. Removed Stand-Up Comedy (41) and Concert/Performance (2) rows: 7,100 → 7,057 rows (4,446 TV shows, 2,611 movies).
  2. Checked missing values: none in Type, Rank, Title, Score, Days or date. (Only the unused Netflix Exclusive column has blanks.)
  3. Converted dates to a date format and added year and month columns.
  4. Standardized categories: the Type column uses only consistent labels, with no spelling or capitalization variants. After step 1 it holds just TV Show and Movie.
  5. Checked duplicates on date + title + rank: none. Five date-title pairs (10 rows) share a cut-off Twilight Saga title with different ranks; they were kept and flagged.
  6. Checked unusual values: no ranks outside 1–10, no scores or days at or below 0, no dates outside the range.
  7. Repaired garbled characters in 21 titles. Repeated titles were kept, because repeat appearances show how long a title stayed popular.

Measures

  • Share of appearances: every day has exactly 10 slots, so a category’s share of slots is the main popularity measure.
  • Rank: 1 is best, 10 is last in the Top 10. A lower average rank means better performance.
  • Days In Top 10: a running count of days a title has been on the chart.
  • Viewership Score: accumulates (11 − rank) points per day on the chart. It is ranking points, not hours or viewers, and it grows with days in the Top 10, so it is not used as separate evidence.

3. Data visualizations

Chart 1: Movies vs. TV shows overall

Of 7,057 movie and TV show appearances, TV shows took 4,446 (63.0%) and movies 2,611 (37.0%). Without the single most frequent title, Cocomelon (428 appearances), TV’s share is still 60.6%.

Chart 2: Popularity trend by month

TV shows led in 23 of 24 months. The only month where movies led was November 2020 (157 movie vs. 133 TV appearances). March 2022 has only 11 days of data. Because every day has 10 slots, monthly totals mainly reflect the number of days; the useful signal is the balance between the lines.

Chart 2b: TV share of appearances by month

This shows the balance directly. Bars start at 0%, the dashed line is 50%, and TV is above it in every month except November 2020 (45.9%, orange). The share ranges from 45.9% to 75.5%. The last bar (March 2022, 11 days) is lighter because it is incomplete.

Chart 3: Average ranking

Lower is better. TV shows averaged rank 5.42 and movies 5.64, a gap of only 0.22 on a 1–10 scale. TV shows also held rank 1 more often (494 times, 11.1% of their appearances, vs. 216 times, 8.3%, for movies).

Chart 4: Time spent in the Top 10

Box = middle 50% of values, line = median, diamond = mean, whiskers = typical range. The dot at the right end marks the maximum. The axis is logarithmic because TV values reach 428 days. Days in Top 10 is the title’s cumulative counter, not always consecutive days. Per-record values repeat each title’s counter on every day it charts, so use the per-title view for comparisons. 3 movies and 7 TV shows were still charting on the last date (March 11, 2022) and 4 movies and 6 TV shows were already charting on the first date (April 1, 2020), so their counts are cut off at one end.

4. Analysis and interpretations

MeasureMoviesTV shows
Entries (share)2,611 (37.0%)4,446 (63.0%)
Distinct titles (approx.)355283
Average / median rank5.64 / 65.42 / 5
Average / median Viewership Score38.9 / 28172.9 / 83
Average / median days in Top 10 (per record)6.0 / 535.0 / 12
Average / median days (per title)7.4 / 616.1 / 9
Most days on chart (cumulative, as observed)31 days428 days
Share of appearances, three unequal windowsApr–Dec 2020: 39.7% · 2021: 35.9% · Jan–Mar 11, 2022: 31.9%Apr–Dec 2020: 60.3% · 2021: 64.1% · Jan–Mar 11, 2022: 68.1%
TV share, like-for-like windowsApr–Dec: 60.3% (2020) vs. 63.4% (2021) · Jan–Mar 11: 68.9% (2021) vs. 68.1% (2022)

The first window covers April–December 2020 only and the last covers January 1 to March 11, 2022 only. Cocomelon’s 428 days are cumulative (August 28, 2020 to March 1, 2022, with gaps) and the title had left the chart before the data ended.

Which category was more popular?

TV shows. They took 63.0% of appearances even though movies had more distinct titles (355 vs. 283). The per-title durations are consistent with TV shows holding their slots longer (median 9 days vs. 6), which probably contributed to the larger share. This analysis does not measure how much of the gap that explains.

Did popularity increase or decrease over time?

The evidence is mixed and does not show a lasting trend. The three windows above are unequal (April–December 2020, all of 2021, January 1–March 11, 2022), so their shares are not directly comparable. Matching the months: TV’s share was 60.3% in April–December 2020 and 63.4% in April–December 2021 (+3.1 points), but 68.9% in January–March 11, 2021 and 68.1% in 2022 (−0.8 points). Month to month the share swung widely (45.9% in November 2020 to 75.5% in October 2021). These are observed shares with no significance test.

Were there months when movies became more popular?

Only one: November 2020. December 2020 (TV 53.9%) and September 2020 (TV 57.0%) were the next closest.

Did TV shows consistently perform better?

It depends on the measure. On appearances, yes: TV led in 23 of 24 months (95.8%). On average rank, only partly: TV had the better monthly average in 16 of 24 months (66.7%), movies had it in 7 (September, October and December 2020; February, May, August and November 2021), and March 2021 was an exact tie (5.50 each). TV consistently took a larger share of Top 10 places, but did not consistently rank higher within the Top 10.

Which stayed popular longer?

TV shows, as observed. The median per title was 9 days vs. 6 for movies. The per-record medians (12 vs. 5) repeat each title’s counter on every day it charts, so treat them as a secondary view. TV’s average (16.1 days per title) is pulled up by a few very long runs (maximum 428 days).

5. Conclusion and recommendations

Answer: On Netflix, between April 2020 and March 2022, TV shows were more popular than movies. They took 63.0% of Top 10 appearances, led in 23 of 24 months, and stayed on the chart longer. The advantage in average rank was small, and movies led in November 2020.

Recommendations

  1. Give TV series priority when deciding what to feature or promote.
    Evidence: 63.0% of Top 10 slots and a TV lead in 23 of 24 months. Uncertainty: these are rankings, not hours watched, and one title (Cocomelon) is 9.6% of TV appearances. Without it TV still holds 60.6%.
  2. Favor titles with staying power over one-off launches.
    Evidence: the median TV title stayed 9 days vs. 6 for movies. Uncertainty: the counts are cumulative and cut off at both ends of the data, so this is consistent with longer holds, not proof of them.
  3. Do not write movies off. Movies led in November 2020 (Chart 2b), and the rank gap is only 0.22.
    Evidence: TV held rank 1 more often (11.1% vs. 8.3% of appearances), yet average ranks are close. Uncertainty: November 2020 is a single month, so study it as a case rather than treating it as a pattern.
  4. Do not forecast a rising TV share from this data.
    Evidence: matched months show +3.1 points in April–December and −0.8 in January–March 11. Uncertainty: two comparisons and no significance test. Track monthly share (Chart 2b) before shifting budget.
  5. Collect hours-watched data before any decision that depends on viewing time. Rankings show popularity on Netflix only, and they say nothing about total viewing or other platforms.

Limitations

  • Data begins in April 2020, so there is no before-and-after COVID-19 comparison, and results cannot be attributed to the pandemic.
  • Data ends March 11, 2022, so 2022 and March 2022 are incomplete.
  • Only Netflix’s Top 10 is covered, not other platforms or actual hours watched.
  • Each daily appearance is a separate record, so repeated titles count every day.
  • The Viewership Score is accumulated ranking points, not hours or viewers.
  • Each day has a fixed 10 slots, so a rise in one category’s share is a fall in the other’s.
  • Days in Top 10 is a cumulative counter. Titles still charting on March 11, 2022 or already charting on April 1, 2020 have counts cut off at one end.
  • The year-to-year shares cover unequal windows and have no uncertainty estimate, so they are descriptive only.
  • One title, Cocomelon, accounts for 428 TV appearances (9.6% of TV). Some titles in the source are cut off, so title counts are approximate.

6. Datasets

Both files are included in full. The cleaned dataset (7,057 movie and TV show rows) is the one used for every chart and statistic above. It adds Year, Month, Year-Month and Partial Month columns, and keeps the repaired Title next to the Title Original, with flags for cut-off titles and for the same title appearing twice in a day. The original dataset (7,100 rows) is the unmodified source file, including the Stand-Up Comedy and Concert/Performance rows that were removed.

This switch changes the table and download only. Every chart and statistic above uses the cleaned dataset.

7. Revised analysis requirements and checks

These requirements come from an independent review of this project. The charts and statistics are fixed snapshots of the cleaned dataset, and the check below recomputes the headline figures from the embedded data each time the page loads.

  1. Period comparisons: report shares for the stated windows, compare matching months only, and make no trend claim from unequal windows.
  2. Duration: use the per-title view as the main comparison, define Days in Top 10 as the cumulative counter, and state which titles are cut off at the first or last date.
  3. Wording: say “consistent with” where the data cannot establish a cause, and describe the 0.22 rank gap as small.
  4. Reproducibility: label summaries as snapshots and confirm that they match the embedded data (below).
  5. Downloads: offer the CSV through a standard browser download and show a message if it fails.
  6. Assignment brief: the MGTS103 scoring form has been applied. The full project brief and its required methods are still unverified.
